ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text:
Gaspar has these seven different pieces, formed by equal little squares.
<image1>
He uses all these pieces to assemble rectangles with different perimeters, that is, with different shapes. How many different perimeters can he find?

ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: In the figure there are seven straight strip-shaped puzzle pieces composed of identical small squares, and their lengths can respectively be counted as 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, and 7 small squares. Reasoning: When all the puzzle pieces are used, the total area is 1+2+3+4+5+6+7=28 small squares. Therefore the area of a rectangle that can be formed must be 28, and the integer side-length combinations of the rectangle are only 1×28, 2×14, and 4×7. Checking these, all can be formed: 1×28 can arrange all long strips end to end in one row; 2×14 can be arranged into two rows, respectively 7+6+1 and 5+4+3+2; 4×7 can be arranged into four rows, respectively 7, 6+1, 5+2, and 4+3. So there are 3 different shapes, corresponding to 3 different perimeters.

raw_record.question_text: Gaspar has these seven different pieces, formed by equal little squares. He uses all these pieces to assemble rectangles with different perimeters, that is, with different shapes. How many different perimeters can he find?

method.method_draft: First describe the image: it shows seven straight bar-shaped pieces made from unit squares, with lengths 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, and 7 squares. From the text, Gaspar must use all seven pieces to form rectangles and count how many different perimeters are possible. Add the unit squares to get total area 1+2+3+4+5+6+7=28. Any rectangle using all pieces must therefore have integer side lengths whose product is 28, so the only unordered dimension pairs are 1×28, 2×14, and 4×7. Verify each can actually be assembled from the bars: 1×28 by placing all bars end to end; 2×14 by making rows 7+6+1 and 5+4+3+2; 4×7 by making rows 7, 6+1, 5+2, and 4+3. These give three distinct perimeters, so the count is 3.

method.method_draft: First describe the image: the pieces are one-square-wide strips containing respectively 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, and 7 equal squares. From the text, all pieces are to be used in complete rectangles, and rectangles with different shapes have different perimeters here. Treat a candidate rectangle as being built from horizontal rows of equal length. The total number of squares is 28, so if the rectangle has h rows, h must divide 28; up to rotation the possible row counts are h=1, 2, and 4. Test these by partitioning the strip lengths into h groups of equal sum: for h=1, all lengths sum to 28; for h=2, split into 14 and 14, for example 7+6+1 and 5+4+3+2; for h=4, split into four sums of 7: 7, 6+1, 5+2, 4+3. Thus exactly three row-count cases produce rectangles: 1×28, 2×14, and 4×7, giving three different perimeters.
